title: Lettre Tate (mai 66) (Cristaux) : lettre (1966), tapuscrit (s.d.), notes manuscrites (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
This page is part of Grothendieck's May 1966 letter to Tate on crystals, §§2.5–2.6. It finishes the discussion of the deformation statement 3º from the previous page. That statement says that lifts B of an abelian scheme A from S to an infinitesimal (PD) thickening T correspond, as an equivalence of categories, to lifts of the Hodge filtration 0 ← R^1f_*O_A ← H^1_DR ← f_*Ω^1 ← 0 to the value DR^1(A/S)(T) of the de Rham crystal. Grothendieck stresses that the Hodge filtration is not crystalline but 'continuous': its variation reflects the variation of the motive. He says firmer foundations for motives, crystals and de Rham cohomology would be needed to make this precise. In today's language this is the contrast between a crystal (rigid, with connection) and the Hodge filtration (moving, Griffiths-transversal), as in variations of Hodge structure and period maps.

He then notes that comparing 3º with Serre–Tate suggests a generalisation to p-divisible and formal groups. Serre–Tate: in characteristic p>0, deforming A is the same as deforming A[p^∞]. He announces this for Chapter 3.

§2.6 gives a group-theoretic model of DR^1(A/S). Over any base, following an old construction of Serre (Rosenlicht–Serre, Groupes algébriques et corps de classes), there is a universal vector extension 0 → V(R^1f_*O_A) → G(A) → A → 0. Here V(E) has sections Hom(E,O_S), so the vector group is ω_{A'} with A' the dual abelian scheme. G(A) is universal among extensions of A by vector bundles, functorial in A, and compatible with base change. Its Lie algebra sits in 0 → (R^1f_*O_A)^∨ = t^∨_{A'} → Lie G(A) → (f_*Ω^1)^∨ = t_A → 0. This is the dual of the Hodge exact sequence, so Lie G(A) ≅ (H^1_DR(A/S))^∨.

The refined assertion 1º is that G is crystalline. For a lift B of A to T, G(B/T) depends up to unique canonical isomorphism only on A and S→T, not on the choice of B. So one gets a crystal of smooth group schemes G(A/S) with G(A/S)(T) ≅ G(B/T).

The next page completes the picture. The quasi-inverse in 3º is: lift the vector subgroup ω_{A'} ⊂ G to a vector subgroup of G(A/S)(T), then take the quotient to get B. There is also the remark about Manin's map via the canonical connection on G. This is exactly the content later written up as Grothendieck–Messing theory (Grothendieck ICM 1970; Messing LNM 264, 1972; Mazur–Messing LNM 370, 1974).
errors: Slip: 'le schéma en groupes G(B/S)' should read G(B/T), since B lives over T. The next page correctly writes G(B/T).
Typo in the original: 'ces sections' should be 'ses sections'.
The machine transcription writes V(R^1f_*(O_{A'})). The image has R^1f_*(O_A), which is correct, because R^1f_*O_A = t_{A'} = Lie of the dual. As transcribed, O_{A'} would be wrong.

Mathematically, 1º and 3º are asserted without proof ('je n'ai pas vérifié'). They hold for PD-thickenings with nilpotent divided powers (Messing). For arbitrary infinitesimal T, the crystal of G must be taken in the crystalline (PD) sense; Grothendieck leaves this implicit here.

ideas.what: The Hodge filtration is not crystalline but a 'continuous' structure whose variation reflects the variation of the motive.
ideas.modern_name: Hodge filtration on the crystal / period map; Griffiths transversality; filtered F-crystals
ideas.where_published: Letter to Tate 1966 (circulated); ICM Nice 1970 'Groupes de Barsotti–Tate et cristaux'

ideas.what: Suggested generalisation via Serre–Tate: deformations of A in char p are deformations of A[p^∞], leading to a crystalline theory for p-divisible and formal groups.
ideas.modern_name: Serre–Tate theorem plus Grothendieck–Messing crystalline Dieudonné theory
ideas.where_published: ICM 1970; Montréal lectures 'Groupes de Barsotti-Tate et cristaux de Dieudonné' (1974)

ideas.what: The universal vector extension of an abelian scheme over any base, extending a construction of Serre. Its Lie algebra is dual to H^1_DR, giving a group-theoretic model of the de Rham crystal.
ideas.modern_name: Universal vector extension E(A), Lie E(A) ≅ H^1_DR(A)^∨
ideas.usually_credited_to: Rosenlicht and Serre (over fields); Mazur–Messing (1974) over general bases
ideas.where_published: Letter to Tate 1966; Mazur–Messing LNM 370 cite Grothendieck

ideas.what: The universal extension is crystalline: G(B/T) is independent of the lift B, up to unique isomorphism, giving a crystal of smooth groups.
ideas.modern_name: Crystalline nature of the universal extension (Mazur–Messing)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Grothendieck; proved by Messing and Mazur–Messing

deep.surprise_reason: This is the well-known source letter of Grothendieck–Messing theory and of the crystalline universal extension. These results are extensively credited to Grothendieck by Messing and Mazur–Messing. The remark crediting Serre and the 'continuous vs crystalline' philosophy are nice historical details but not new to specialists.
